items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread, matzah), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (and for Reform Jews worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora for Orthodox and Conservative Jews.

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night in the Diaspora). The Haggadah ('the telling') is recited — recounting the Exodus through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions (asked by the youngest).

The festival ends with 'Next year in Jerusalem'. Its liberation theme has shaped social movements: African American spirituals (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), Latin American liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.

items.title: Aristotelian virtue ethics aims at eudaimonia, not just being virtuous
items.claim: What is eudaimonia in Aristotle's ethics?

options.text: Flourishing or living well — the proper end of human life. The virtues (excellences of character) are dispositions that enable a person to function well as a human being and so to live a flourishing life

items.reveal:
Aristotle's 'Nicomachean Ethics' (Book I) argues that all human action aims at some good, and there must be a highest good — eudaimonia.

The ergon (function) argument: humans, like everything, have a characteristic function — rational activity according to virtue. The virtues are not lists of good behaviours but stable dispositions developed through habituation.

The doctrine of the mean: each virtue is between two vices (courage between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between miserliness and profligacy).

Alasdair MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' (1981) revived virtue ethics by arguing that modern moral discourse has lost the framework that gives moral vocabulary its meaning.
items.why: Virtue ethics is not 'be a good person'. It is a structured theory with specific terms — function, habituation, the mean, flourishing — that link character to the good life in a way that act-based theories don't.

items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India
The Khalsa (the 'pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and gender
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surname Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women — symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers that emerged from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.
